newsitem.title: MEXICO: Colombia slams Mexico and Guatemala on coffee trade.
newsitem.headline: Colombia slams Mexico and Guatemala on coffee trade.

text.p: Colombia took a public swipe at Mexico and Guatemala on Saturday for failing to support efforts to boost world coffee prices by curbing their exports.

Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo led the attack, saying the two countries were "destabilizing forces" in the world market and undermining efforts by Colombia and other members of the Association of Coffee Exporting Countries (ACPC) to win better prices for all producers.
"In my opinion, these two nations represent the greatest threat to Colombia since, in reality, it is they who are determining the behavior of our prices on the international market," Ocampo said.

He said Mexico and Guatemala had increased their coffee exports by 30 percent over the last year, at the same time that Colombia, Brazil and other ACPC-member countries were voluntarily limiting their sales as part of an export retention scheme aimed at pressuring consumers and traders on world commodity markets to raise prices.
The ACPC agreed last May to limit green coffee exports from its members, who account for anywhere between 70 and 80 percent of world supply, to 53.5 million 60-kilo bags in the year to June 1997.

Mexico and Guatemala are not members of the ACPC, and Ocampo -- who spoke in an address to the annual meeting of Colombia's National Coffee Exporters' Association -- said their boycott was effectively undermining its efforts to win better prices.

Colombia, especially, had been put at a serious disadvantage in the global marketplace because of the boycott, Ocampo said, arguing Mexico and Guatemala have lower production costs and are therefore in a better position to ride out any slump in world prices.

Jorge Cardenas, the head of Colombia's powerful National Coffee Growers' Federation, agreed with Ocampo, saying it was "disillusioning" to see other countries take advantage of the retention plan to boost their market share.

He ruled out a possible collapse of the ACPC plan because of it, however, saying member countries were strong enough and controlled a sufficient amount of the world market to ensure the plan prospers over the long term.
